system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2141-10-18 23:40:00 to 2141-10-21 17:49:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of recurrent left leg cellulitis, venous stasis ulcers, lipodermatosclerosis, and multiple comorbidities was admitted due to worsening erythema, pain, and swelling in her left leg over the prior 24 hours. She had recently discontinued doxycycline after outpatient improvement, but symptoms recurred. IV vancomycin was initiated, and pain was managed with oxycodone after a morphine allergy reaction. She remained afebrile with stable labs and improving clinical signs. Imaging ruled out necrotizing infection, septic joint, and DVT. The rash that developed on admission was attributed to contact dermatitis. She transitioned to oral doxycycline at discharge with plans for infectious disease follow-up, and was advised to continue compression, elevation, and all chronic medications including iron supplementation and Creon. She was discharged home in stable condition.
problems: Cellulitis and abscess of leg, except foot
Ulcer of other part of lower limb
Other opiates and related narcotics causing adverse effects in therapeutic use
Spinal stenosis, lumbar region, without neurogenic claudication
Unspecified hereditary and idiopathic peripheral neuropathy
Contact dermatitis and other eczema, unspecified cause
Osteoarthrosis, unspecified whether generalized or localized, site unspecified
Diverticulosis of colon (without mention of hemorrhage)
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

was trended through hospitalization and remained stable.

not tolerate iron supplementation.  She should follow up as an 
outpatient with a rescheduled colonoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. My left leg has been getting worse—more red, swollen, and painful over the last few days. I’ve been on doxycycline, but it’s not helping. It started weeping today, so I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had this before, right—recurrent cellulitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, usually in the same spot. I wrap it daily and clean it, but this time it just keeps getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve started you on IV vancomycin for the infection. We also did an ultrasound to check for a blood clot, and it came back negative for DVT, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about another clot since I’ve had one before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also giving you oxycodone for pain and will keep an eye on your leg. You’re not running a fever, which is a good sign the infection isn’t spreading systemically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel nauseous though—could that be from the doxycycline?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s a common side effect. Since you’re having trouble with it, we’re stopping doxycycline and will switch to a different oral antibiotic later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. What will I be on instead?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re waiting on infectious disease to recommend the best option. But likely minocycline, which is similar but often better tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable—white count is normal, and no signs of anemia worsening. The vancomycin is working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My leg feels a little less tight today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. The redness is starting to improve. We’ll keep the IV antibiotics going for a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my iron? I know it’s low, but I can’t take the pills without getting sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your iron studies—it confirms iron deficiency. But because of your chronic pancreatitis, your stomach doesn’t handle oral iron well. We’ll hold off on the pills and reschedule your colonoscopy as an outpatient to check for sources of blood loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been putting that off because of the leg, but I know I need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s important. We’ll get it rescheduled once you’re feeling better. For now, we’re continuing your B12 injections and vitamin D.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The infectious disease team reviewed your case. They recommend switching to minocycline by mouth. We’ll stop the IV vancomycin tomorrow if you keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll be on minocycline instead of doxycycline?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s in the same family but tends to cause less nausea. You’ll take it twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll stop the doxycycline completely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve already stopped it. You’ll start minocycline today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. My stomach feels better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your pancreatitis symptoms have improved since stopping doxycycline. Keep taking your Creon with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nurse said something about a compression dressing. What’s that for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the wound care team will apply a compression bandage tomorrow before discharge. It helps reduce swelling and supports healing in your leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long do I wear it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Three days. Then you’ll remove it and use Adaptic and Kerlix dressings until your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I need to see the wound clinic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll monitor the healing. Also, you have an appointment with infectious disease to manage your long-term antibiotic plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home today. Your infection has improved, and you’re tolerating the minocycline well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the minocycline twice daily. Stop the doxycycline completely. Use acetaminophen or oxycodone as needed for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the compression bandage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep it on for three days. Then switch to the Adaptic and Kerlix. The instructions are written down for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still on my Mirapex for restless legs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue Mirapex. Also keep using your inhaler for asthma, and the nasal spray for allergies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And iron? Should I try the pills again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try taking it with food to reduce nausea. If it still bothers you, call your doctor. But it’s important to keep trying, especially with your history of anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if the leg gets more red, painful, or if you develop a fever. Otherwise, keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m glad I came in when I did.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Me too. You did the right thing. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of recurrent left leg cellulitis, venous insufficiency, and lipodermatosclerosis was admitted due to worsening erythema, pain, and weeping in her left lower extremity despite doxycycline therapy. She was started on IV vancomycin and transitioned to minocycline after consultation with infectious disease. Her infection improved during the hospital stay, and a compression dressing was applied at discharge. She was advised to remove it in three days and follow up with wound care and infectious disease. Iron deficiency anemia was noted, but oral supplementation was poorly tolerated due to chronic pancreatitis; colonoscopy was rescheduled as an outpatient. She remained stable, with pain managed using acetaminophen and oxycodone, and was discharged home with clear instructions on medication changes and wound care.
